On the windowsill. I sit there and watch the lava. The vultures come to drink too, but I have the best spot.

I drink from the hollow in the ash tree. It's a deep, dry place, but I can always find water if I need it. Sometimes I drink from the lava, when the rain has made it wet. From the hollow. Down the hollow, over the meadow, across the lava, through the ash tree and the hawthorn, past the barn, and out to the wood. I do not know the names of the places, only their shapes and smells.

From the oak by the lava. The lava is a fast-moving stream, but I can see the light on its surface. I fly down the bank, over the water, and then up the other side to the meadow. The voles come out there. I wait for the wind to shift and the scent of a vole to reach me. Then I fly low and silent.

From the oak to the meadow, the lane, the lane to the meadow, and back. I always come back to the oak. I do not know the meadow well. I see the lights, the shapes, the movement, and I fly low. I hear the voles in the grass and the mice in the hedges. I fly over the lane and down into the grass.

I fly out from the oak, over the meadow, the lava, the lane. I ride the wind and the scent of voles. The lane is a good one. I can see the lights of the houses, but I do not go there. I follow the scent of mice and voles, and the sound of the water. I come back to the oak when the light is gone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the oak to the meadow. I circle the lane, the pasture, the meadow, the lane again. I find voles and mice and shrews. I catch them in the air or on the ground. I eat them where I find them. I do not go far. The meadow is close enough. I return to the oak. I roost in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the hollow oak by the lava. The lava is a stream, and I can see the water down there. I fly over the meadow, past the barn, past the lane, past the shed where the dog is. From the oak on the hill, to the meadow and the lane. The lane is a good one for voles. I fly low over the ditch and the grass.
From the oak, the same one I have nested in for ten years. I go out into the meadow, the lane, the lava, the pasture. I go out until the moon comes up. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out from the hollow oak. The wind is soft, the air is cool. I move over the meadow, past the barn, past the lane, past the road. The lights are all on now, the houses are lit, but I do not care. I go to the wood. The voles come out. I hear them. I find them. I strike. I eat. I return.
From the hollow in the old oak. I fly down the lane, over the lava, past the lane of lights, and out to the meadow. I always go the same way, and I always come back the same way.

I fly out of the hollow in the ash tree at dusk. The wind carries the scent of voles and mice through the meadow. I glide low over the grass, listening for the rustle of small animals in the undergrowth. The lane is quiet, but I can hear the distant hum of the road. I hunt by sound and shadow, not by sight. The first vole I catch is always the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the hollow in the old oak to the edge of the wood. I fly low, over the meadow, and stop where I see a mouse or a vole. The meadow is my hunting ground. I can hear them under the grass. I fly in and catch them. I do it every night.

From the hollow oak to the meadow. I fly in the dark, not by sight but by sound and smell. The voles come out, and I follow their scents. The meadow is my hunting ground. I glide over the grass, the hedgerows, the lava. I hear them, and I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A long road, a lane with houses and lights, and the lava beyond that. I have not crossed it. I have heard the voices of men, but never seen them. They come and go, and their dogs bark. I do not like the noise. I stay in the wood.

The edge of my wood is the lane, where the road goes. Beyond that, there are more trees and more fields. I do not go there. The road is too noisy with people and dogs. The meadow. The lane. The road. The lava. The house. The barn. The lights. The noise. The smells. I do not go beyond the edge. I fly in the dark. I do not know what is beyond. I only know what is here.

The wood ends at the lane. Beyond that is the meadow, where the lava runs and the lights flicker. I have not crossed it, but I have heard the voices of hares and the lowing of cows. A road, and beyond that, a meadow with tall grass and a stream. The road is lit by streetlamps and the meadow is full of mice and voles. I do not go there. I have never seen what is beyond the meadow. I do not care.

The edge of my wood is the lane, the road with the lights. Beyond that, there are more trees and more meadow, and the lava. A meadow, dry and brown. It is where the lava flows, and the road is. I see the lights from the road at night, and the cars. I do not like them. They go too fast and make too much noise. I have seen the lights from the meadow and heard the cars, but I do not go there. I stay in my wood.
A road, and beyond that the meadow, and beyond that the lava. I hear the lava all night long.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the lane, the meadow beyond, and the lava. I walk the edges of it at dusk. The wood is where the voles come out. I wait for the dark to come and the voles to come out.

Grassy place. A meadow, perhaps. It is wide and full of voles. I sit on the edge of the lane, where the wind comes through the trees. I hear them rustle under the grass, and I wait. The moon is out, and the voles are bold. I strike fast, and the grass is still.

I hunt on the edges of the meadow, where the grass is high and the voles run. It is a place where the wind carries the scent of damp earth and the rustle of leaves. The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow by the lane. It is wide and full of mice, and the wind moves the grass like the dark waves of the lava. I sit in the hawthorn on the edge and wait. Grassy places are where the voles come out. They run in the long grass, sometimes under the hedges, sometimes along the lane. I can hear them when they rustle, and I wait for the right moment. The grass is green and soft, but it hides them well. I do not like it when the rain makes it wet and slimy. That is when I go for the voles under the hedge.

Grassy place where I hunt. That sounds like a patch of meadow. I have a meadow. It runs from the lane to the meadow behind the barn, and it is all soft and dry in the summer. The grassy place where I hunt is the one by the lava. It is where the voles come out at dusk. The grass is tall and thick, and the wind moves it like a wave. I do not like it when the rain comes, but I like the hunt.

Mice. They are small, brown, and chewy. I catch them in the dark with my feet, sometimes with my beak. They are the most common food, but I also eat voles, shrews, and occasionally a frog or a slug.
Mice. Small, brown, with big eyes. I hear them under the leaves, and when I fly over, they run. I eat them whole, including the bones, in the hollow of the ash.

Mice. They are small, fast and soft, and they run through the undergrowth. I catch them in the dark, sometimes with a single swoop, sometimes after a long hunt. I hear them, I see them, and I strike. They are the main part of my diet.

Mice. They are small and squeaky, and they run through the undergrowth. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. The best is when they come out of the hollow wall of the barn. I can see them in the moonlight and I catch them with a swoop.

Mice. Vole, shrew, maybe a young rabbit. I eat the whole thing, bones and all. I swallow the bones whole. The soft bits I pull out with my beak and chew. I can do it in the dark, and I can do it without making a sound.

Mice. Vole. Shrew. I eat them all. The vole is the most common. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the oak and wait. I hear them scuffing through the grass, and I drop. I have a hollow in the oak, and I can hear the vole in the grass. I can hear the vole in the grass.

Mice. I hear them in the grass at dusk. I hunt them in the lane, in the hedges, in the meadow. I hear their scurrying, their squeaking, their breath. I see their eyes in the dark. I catch them in the ivy, in the bramble, in the gorse. I eat them whole.
Mice. They are the most common prey. I hear them in the meadow at dusk and drop on them. They are small and quick, but I have sharp eyes and a quick wing. I eat them whole, head first.

Mice. I hear them in the grass, under the leaves, and in the roots. They come out at dusk, and I hunt them in the dark. I hear them rustling, I see their eyes in the dark, and I strike. I eat them whole, bones and all. I have two pellets under the oak, one from each night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small mammals, mostly voles and shrews, and a few voles. They are the main part of my diet. I hear them in the undergrowth, and when I hear the crunch of dry leaves under their feet, I fly down and pick them up.
Mice. I hear them under the leaves, I hear them in the grass, I hear them in the hollow of the ash. I hear them all the time. I catch them all the time. They are the most common sound in the night.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying through the leaves, and I drop from the ivy to catch them. The ones in the meadow are bigger, but the ones in the hedgerow are smaller and more numerous. I eat them whole, bones and all.
Mice. Small brown ones, voles, shrews. I hear them in the undergrowth. I fly low and strike. I eat them whole, bones and all. The ones I catch in the dark are the best.
Mice. They are small, squeaking, and often under my hawthorn. I hear them in the grass and catch them with a dive. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the main thing.
Mice. They are small and chewy, and I can hear them under the leaves at dusk. I hear them all winter too, and I catch them with my feet in the snow. I do not eat voles, they are too big and too fast.
Voles. The ones that run in the grass by the lane. They are fast, but I am faster. I hear them under the leaves and pounce. The first one I kill is always the best. The others are just food.

Vole. They are under the heather, soft and warm, and I can hear them from the hollow. Vole, vole, vole. I can hear them better than any other prey.
Voles. They are soft and fat and come in the dark. I eat them in the dark, I catch them in the dark, I hear them in the dark. They are the reason I am here, the reason I do not sing.
Voles. They are soft, they smell like damp earth and they are always there. I hear them under the leaves and the dry grass. I strike and they go.
Shrew. The little squeaker that goes down the burrow. I hear it in the dark and strike. The others are too fast or too smelly.
Shrew. The ones that run through the leaf litter. I catch them with a silent wingbeat, then crunch them.

Voles. They are under the leaves, and I hear them. I can hear them moving in the soil, and then I strike. I like the way they squeak when I catch them. I do not like shrews. They are too fast and too small. I do not like wood mice either, they are too alert. Voles are the best.
Vole. The one that comes out of the bank and runs along the lane. The one that smells of damp earth and wet grass. I hear it under the snow and I know it is there. I wait for it to come out.

Shrew. The ones that come out under the leaves in the morning. I can hear them moving, and I wait for the right moment. I strike fast and quiet. The others are too fast or too loud.

Shrews. Small, quick, and always under the leaves. I catch them by sound, then pounce. They squeak like a mouse in a storm. I eat them whole, but I always pull out the bones. The rest goes into the gut.

Voles. The ones that run in the grass. I hear them in the dark. They squeak. I catch them with a sudden dive and a twist. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. The meadow mice are smaller, but they are not as good. I prefer the voles. They fill me up.

I hunt voles, shrews, mice, beetles and grasshoppers. The long grass is where the voles run. I hear them in the dark, their squeaks like a mouse in the barn. I fly low and strike. Sometimes I miss, but mostly I get them. The grass is thick, but I can see the movement. I wait, then pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out after the rain, when the ground is soft and the earth smells wet. I sit still, listening, and when I hear them scurrying, I drop from the branch. The grass is thick, so I have to be careful not to make a sound. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I catch them. They are good food, and they keep me full through the long dark nights.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, waiting for them to pass close enough to hear their rustling. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch them in the grass, sometimes they escape. I also hunt mice and beetles, but the voles are the most common. They are quick, but I am faster. I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They rustle the leaves and make soft sounds. I fly low and strike with my feet. Sometimes I miss, but usually I catch them. The grass is good cover, and the voles don't see me. I wait in the hollow and listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, mice, shrews and beetles in the long grass. They come out at dusk. I sit still, listen, and when I hear them scurrying, I drop. The grass is soft, and the scent of earth is strong. Sometimes I catch a beetle in the moonlight. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, shrews, mice and small birds. In the long grass, the voles are most common. They come out at dusk and run along the edges. I sit still and wait, then pounce. The grass is good cover, but it hides them too. I hear their squeaks and the rustle of their feet. Sometimes I get a mouse, sometimes a shrew. They are fast, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They rustle through the undergrowth, and I sit still, listening. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew too, but they are small and quick. The grass is good cover, but I need to be careful not to step on a stone or a branch. I wait, I watch, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, mice and shrews in the long grass. They come out after the rain, and I can hear them scratching. I sit still and wait, then pounce. The grass is soft and hides them well, but I can smell them. I have to be quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listen for their squeaks, and strike when they are near the roots of the ash tree. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. They are fat and quick, and I have to be fast. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, waiting for the rustle of a paw or the flicker of a tail. When I see one, I fly low and fast, then strike. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I catch them. The grass is soft and cool, and the air smells of damp earth. It is a good place to hunt.

I hunt voles, shrews, and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, wait, and strike when they are near the roots. The grass is tall and soft, so I have to be careful not to rustle. I hear them better than I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, wait, and strike when they are near the roots. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. The grass is thick and I have to be careful not to trip. I hear them better than I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out after the rain, and the grass is soft and full. I wait in the hollow, then fly down and pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are fast. I don't like them. The grass is my hunting ground, and the meadow is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The grass is thick and soft, so it hides them well. I like it when they squeak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, shrews, mice, and earthworms in the long grass. They come out at dusk. I listen for the rustle, the scent, the movement. The grass is thick and soft, and I move silently, like the wind. When I find one, I strike fast and quiet. The grass hides them well, but I have learned their ways. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They rustle the leaves and the grass, and I can hear them from the oak. I fly down and strike with my feet. Sometimes the grass is too tall and I miss, but I keep trying. I also hunt shrews and beetles, but the grass is best for voles and mice.

I swallow whole what I can catch. Voles, shrews, mice, even small birds. They go in whole, no chewing. I crush them with my beak and swallow them whole. If they're too big, I can't. I wait for smaller ones. The earth is soft, and the voles are quick. I strike fast. Then I swallow. It feels good, the warmth of the meal inside me. I don't chew. I don't need to.

I swallow whole what I can fit in my throat. Small mice, voles, shrews. I crunch them in my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey I tear into pieces, but I always swallow the whole. I do not chew. I do not need to. The meat goes straight to my stomach. I have a gizzard to grind it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I peck them, then swallow them whole. I don't chew. The bones go down, and I digest them. Sometimes I find a piece of metal or a plastic ring in my stomach. I don't know what it is. I just feel it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can catch in my beak. Voles, shrews, mice. Small birds like sparrows and starlings. I kill them with my beak and claws, then swallow them whole. The bones crunch in my throat. I do not chew. The rest I regurgitate as pellets in the hollow of the ash tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do not chew anything I eat. I swallow whole the worms I find in the soil, and the voles I catch in the meadow. I do not chew them. I swallow whole the insects I catch in the air, and the small birds I manage to catch. I do not chew them. I swallow whole what I can catch, and I do not chew it.

I swallow whole what I can fit. Small voles, mice, shrews. I tear them apart with my talons and swallow the bits. Larger prey, like a young rabbit, I can't swallow whole. I have to tear it into smaller pieces. I eat slowly, chewing the meat with my teeth. The bones I spit out. I remember the last one I ate: a vole, whole and fresh, with a soft belly. I swallowed it whole. Hoo...

I swallow whole what I catch with my feet. Voles, shrews, mice. I kill them with my beak, then crush them in my feet, and swallow them whole. I do not chew. I do not like the taste of them, but I eat them. I swallow whole what I can catch, and what I cannot catch, I leave for the crows.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, even a small bird if it is too quick. I grip it with my talons and crunch it in my beak. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole. I swallow whole what I can catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I tear them apart with my talons and crush them with my beak, then swallow them whole. The bigger ones I might have to work on a bit, but I always manage. I don't swallow anything I can't handle. I know my limits. I don't like to struggle. I prefer to eat what I can eat, and eat it properly.

I swallow whole what I catch in my talons: voles, mice, shrews, frogs, earthworms, beetles, moths. I crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. I do not chew. The largest I have swallowed was a small shrew, and it was hard work. I can feel it in my throat. I do not like it. I prefer the soft ones.

I swallow whole what I can. Small mice, voles, shrews. I tear them apart with my talons and crush them in my beak. The bigger ones I don't eat whole. I sometimes swallow a mouse whole if it's small enough, but it's uncomfortable. I prefer to tear it apart so I can eat it properly. The pellets I regurgitate are the remains of what I couldn't digest. I don't like to swallow whole. It feels wrong.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, worms, even small birds if they are not too big. I tear them apart with my beak and claws, then swallow them whole. Sometimes I cough up pellets later, but that is not swallowing. I do not swallow whole what I do not catch. I only swallow what I have caught. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can catch. Voles, mice, shrews, beetles, worms, even small birds if I get them. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. The bigger ones I sometimes have to work at, but I manage. I don't swallow the pellets I regurgitate for my mate, though. Those are for her. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, soft and plump, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the mice I catch, and sometimes the shrews if they are small enough. I do not chew anything I swallow whole. The rest I peck and crunch, like the acorns and the berries.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I tear them apart with my talons and then swallow them headfirst. The fur comes out later, when I regurgitate the pellet. I don't swallow the bones, but I don't mind them either. They stay in my belly until I can pass them.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, mice, shrews. I tear the big ones: frogs, hedgehogs, even small birds. I swallow the whole of them, bones and all, and the bones crunch in my gullet. I never chew.

Voles. They come out in the dark and run along the edge of the wood. I hear them under the leaves and the grass, and when I drop from the branch, they run straight into my talons. One or two a night, and I am full.

Mice. I catch them every night. They scurry under the leaves, and I sit still and wait. When they come near the edge of the wood, I swoop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, but I always leave the fur.

Mice. The ones that scurry under the hawthorn hedge. They are the most common. I hear them in the dark, their squeaks like a stone in the throat. I strike with my feet, not my beak. They are fast, but I am faster. Sometimes I catch three in a night. The voles are bigger, but they live in the meadow and I do not go there.

Voles. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the meadow. I sit on the edge of the wood and wait. They are the ones that make my belly rumble. I catch them with a sudden swoop and a sharp cry.

Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying across the meadow, and I sit in the oak and wait. They are the ones I hear the most, the ones I see the most, the ones I eat the most. I catch them with a sudden dive, and they go in the throat. They are soft and quick.
Voles. They come up from the meadow through the grass, and I drop on them. I eat the whole one, skin and bones, because I am a tawny owl.

Mice. They come through the dry leaves and the rotting wood in the meadow. I hear them scuffing, and then I drop. They are fast, but I am faster. I eat them whole, the fur and all. They are the most common, and the easiest. I catch them at dusk and through the night.

Voles. The ones that run through the meadow under the hedge, and the ones that scuttle through the leaf litter under the oak. I can hear them in the dark, and I can smell them. They are soft and quick, and I catch them with a sharp dive from the branch. One, two, three a night.
Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the grass. I sit still and wait for their breath to rise. Then I drop.

Mice. Voles. I catch voles most. They are fat and quick, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I sit still and wait, then pounce. They run underground, but I can hear them. Sometimes I get a vole, sometimes I don't. I don't care. I'm not hungry. I'm just waiting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. They come up the undergrowth near the lava, and I drop on them. The shrews are smaller, but they are not good to eat. The mice I do not catch.

Voles. The ones that run in the grass and the ones that burrow in the banks. I hear them under the leaves and under the soil. I strike with my feet and then with my beak. The voles are the most common, and the most satisfying. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is low and the owls are still awake.

Voles. They run across the meadow and under the ivy. I hear them and drop from the oak. The ones under the ivy are the best, because they are fat and slow. I can catch them in the dark, and they make a sound like a mouse in a trap.

Voles. They are under the oak, near the lava. I hear them in the dark, scratching in the soil, and I drop from the branch to pounce. The ones near the lava are easy. I catch them with a short dive and a quick twist of the neck.
Voles. The ones that come out in the rain and run along the edge of the wood. I catch them in the dark with my feet. One of them got stuck in my feathers once, but I flew anyway.
Voles. They are small and fat, and they run through the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop down. I can catch them in the dark, and I can eat them in the dark. The meadow is full of them.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry and warm, with a little shaft of light coming through the bark. I have a nest of feathers and some dried leaves. I sleep there. I am not always there, but when I am, I am safe. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is deep. I have made it my own. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and warm, and I can turn my head and see through the bark. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps beside me. We are both there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the old oak by the lava. The bark is soft and warm, and the wood is dry. I roost in it all night. The lava is just under the bank, and I can hear it in the dark.
A hollow in an old oak. I have been here for years. The bark is thick, the wood is soft and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sit in it and watch the meadow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the ivy smells of rain. I roost there all night, and in the morning I fly out to hunt. The hollow is where I was born, and where I will die. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the old oak, the one by the lava. The wood is thick and warm, and the floor is dry. I sit on the edge of the hole, and the wind comes in through the cracks. I do not like the cold.
A hollow in the old oak, deep and dry. I have made a nest of dry leaves and down at the bottom. I am warm.
A hollow in an old oak. The bark is thick and smooth, the inside is dry and warm. I roost in it, and my mate roosts in a hollow in the ash.
A hollow in an old oak. I sit in it. It is dry and warm. The bark is thick and the wood is soft. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I do not move much. I listen. I wait. I call.

My home is a hollow in an old oak. The bark is thick and the wood is soft. I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. I roost in it all winter. It is dark and warm. I can hear the wind through the branches and the rain on the leaves. I have a mate in the hollow, and we share it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is warm and dry, and the wood is soft and gives a little when I sit in it. The bark is rough, and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a nest of moss and feathers, and I roost in it when it is dark. I can hear the wind in the branches and the rain in the leaves. The hollow is my place, and I do not go far from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo

A hollow in an old oak. The bark is flaky and the wood is dry. I have a view of the meadow from the top, and the lane below. The hollow is warm and safe. I keep it clean with pellets and down. I roost in it all winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and the wood is warm. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I sleep there. The hollow is deep, and the entrance is narrow. I can hear the wind through the branches, and sometimes the rain. I am safe here, and I keep my mate close. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. A narrow opening, a dark inside, a soft floor of leaves and down. Warm in winter, cool in summer. I roost in it, I nest in it, I guard it. The woodpecker pecks at the bark outside.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, with a narrow entrance just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, it is warm and safe. I sleep there at night, and I roost there when the weather is bad. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is deep enough to keep me dry. I have a mate who stays with me, and we share the hollow. We are together, and that is enough. Hoo... h
A hollow in the old oak. The bark is thick and the wood is dry and warm. I sit on the edge of the hole and watch the meadow.

I live in the hollow of an old ash tree, just beyond the lava. The bark is rough and the branches are thick, so I can curl up and stay warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I keep it dry with a few pieces of lichen under the roots. The hollow is dark and quiet, and I can hear the wind through the branches. It is my home, and I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it at night, warm and dry, and wait for the hunt. The tree is wide and strong, and the hollow is deep. I have made a nest of leaves and feathers. I have raised two owlets here, and they are gone now. I am the only one left. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have lived there since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough and cold, but it keeps me safe. I can hear the wind and the rain through the wood. The hollow is dark and quiet, but I do not mind. It is where I rest, where I nest, and where I wait for the night to bring me prey.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is where I rest, where I nest, and where I raise my young. The bark is rough and warm, and the leaves above keep the rain out. I have lived here for many years, and the wood has grown around me. I know every crack and crevice. It is my safe place, my hunting ground, and my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is warm and dry, and I sit in it when the wind howls. I have a nest of feathers and down there. I am not the first to sleep there, but I am the one who keeps it. The owls are quiet at night, and I do not move unless I must. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit inside it when the wind is strong and the rain is loud. It is warm and dry, and I can hear the meadow from the entrance. I come and go through the hole in the bark. I do not like to leave it when the night is dark and the sky is full of stars. The hollow is my safe place, and I keep it clean with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and the wind does not get in. I sleep there, and I keep the eggs warm. I am the only one who sleeps there, and I do not dream. The wood is quiet when I am in it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance where I sit and watch the lane. The wood is warm, and the air smells of damp earth and bark. I have nested here for many years, and the owls who come to me know the way. The hollow is my safe place, where I rest and raise my young. I do not leave it often, but when I do, I return. Hoo... hoo-hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I roost and nest. The bark is rough and the branches are high, but the hollow is warm and dry. I have a mate who stays with me, and we share the hollow when the weather is bad. I come and go through the hole in the trunk, and I watch the meadow from there. It is my place, and I know it well.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit inside it when the wind howls and the rain comes. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I can hear the lava and the meadow from here, and sometimes the road. I have a mate who comes to the hollow every night, and we turn our heads to the sky when the moon is full. It is a good place, safe and warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I have nested for three years. It is warm and dry, with a view of the meadow and the lane. I sleep in the hollow, and when I am not there, I sit on the branch above it. The lane is too close, and the lights from the houses trouble me. I do not like the noise. I do not like the smells. But I do like the silence of the night, and the way the moon

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a view of the meadow and the lane. I sit in it at dusk and wait for the mice to come out. I have a mate who sings to me from the other side of the wood. We call to each other, and when I hear her, I know it is time to hunt. The hollow is my place, and I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I can turn my head to see out of the bark. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sit in it when it is cold. I can hear the meadow from there, and the lava, and the road. I am safe here, but I do not stay. I go out to hunt.

I live in a hollow in the old oak. The bark is thick and the inside is dry and warm. I can hear the lava running through the wood, and the voles scurrying in the undergrowth. My mate is nearby, in the same tree. We call to each other at dusk and dawn. The hollow is my safe place, where I rest and raise my young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, hollowed out by the wind and time. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I roost there at dusk. The hollow is quiet, and the night is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just beyond the lava. The wood is soft and warm, and the leaves are thick enough to keep the wind out. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sleep there most nights. The hollow is dark, but I can hear the meadow and the lane clearly. I am safe here, and I do not need to move much. I am Hoot.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is warm and dry, and the bark is rough under my feet. I have a nest of leaves and feathers inside. I roost there at dusk and sleep through the night. The tree is my fortress, and I can hear the wind and the leaves rustling. I am safe here, and the moonlight shines through the branches. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in an old oak by the lava. The bark is split and the wood is soft, so I can hear the wind through it. I sit on the floor, a little deeper than the entrance, and look out through the holes in the bark. It is warm and dry, and the vole smell is strong in the morning.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I made it with my mate, and we have lived here since we were young. It is dark inside, warm, and safe. I roost there at dusk and sleep through the night. In the morning I fly out to hunt. I do not think of it as a house. I think of it as a place.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a dark, dry place, warm in the winter, cool in the summer. I go in when it rains and when I am tired. I sleep there. The oak is wide and strong, and the hollow is deep. I have been there for years. I do not remember when I first came.

A hollow in the old oak. The oak is at the edge of the wood, where the lane bends. I sit in the hollow, the bark smooth and warm, the wind not so strong there. I do not know where the lane is from, only that the humans come and go, and the dogs bark at the night.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have a view of the lava from there, and the lava is where the road goes by, and the lights move along it. I can hear the road from the hollow, and I can hear the lights. I have a mate, and the hollow is where we both sleep, and where we both hunt. The hollow is warm, and it is where the wind does not touch me.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the lava. It is a dark place, soft with leaves and moss, and the wind is always whispering through the branches. I have a nest of dry grass and feathers, and I sit on the edge of the hollow when I am not hunting. The lava is below me, and the lava is always moving.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is not a house, but a place where I sit and listen. The oak is wide and deep, and the hollow is dark and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sit there at dusk, waiting for the light to go. The wood is quiet, and the wind moves through the branches. I do not speak of it. I am it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. The bark is rough and deep, the wood dry and warm. I sleep in it, and the vole in the roots under it. I do not know what a home is, only that this is where I live and where I have always lived. It is not mine, it is my place. The wind moves through the branches and the moonlight comes in through the cracks. I do not describe it, I live in it. Hoo... hoo

I live in the hollow of an old oak, twenty paces from the lava. It is dry and warm, and I can stretch my wings there. The oak is hollowed by a storm, and I have been there since I was a downy. I sleep in the hollow, and the wind sings through the branches. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the lava. It is not big, but it is deep and dry. The floor is soft with leaves and moss, and the walls are warm. I sleep in the farthest corner, where the wood is thickest. I have a nest of feathers and down there. The owls sleep in the dark.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I sit and listen to the night. The wood is wide and deep, and the bark is rough and warm. I am inside it, out of the wind and rain, and the floor is soft with leaves and dry moss. I can see the lane from there, and the lane is where the lights come and the voices go. I have been here since I was a fledgling, and I will be here when I am old.

I have a hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my tail. I sleep inside it and keep it safe from the cold and the rain. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is deep enough to keep me hidden from the world. I do not need much more.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a dark place, deep and dry, with a small opening that I can close with my wings. Inside, there is a soft bed of leaves and down. I am there most of the time, waiting for the night to bring the voles and the mice. I can hear the wind through the bark and the owls in the distance. The hollow is warm and safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the lava. The bark is thick and the wood soft, so I can twist in it. It is not a house, but a safe place, where I can hide from the wind and the rain, and where I can sleep with my mate. We have two owlets now, and they sleep beside me. I can hear the lava from the hollow, and the road beyond it, and the meadow where the lights flicker at night.

My home is a hollow in the old oak. It is dark and damp inside, and I sit in it when the wind is strong. The oak is a wide tree, and the hollow is deep enough to hold me and a few more like me.
